article.title: How to Fix a Leaky Faucet by Replacing the Cartridge
article.summary: Stop a dripping single-handle faucet: identify the cartridge, shut off the water, remove the handle, swap the cartridge in the right position and test.
article.body:
A drip from a single-handle kitchen or bathroom faucet usually means a worn cartridge, the part inside that mixes hot and cold. Replacing it fixes the drip and makes the handle feel new. This guide covers the common cartridge faucets from brands like Moen, Delta and Pfister.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: shut off both water supply valves and open the faucet to relieve pressure before you take anything apart. Plug the drain so small parts can't fall in.

Steps

  1. Identify the faucet and cartridge

    Look for the brand name on the faucet and find the model in the paperwork, the maker's website or by photo. Many manufacturers offer lifetime warranties on cartridges for the original owner, so contact them before buying one.

    Done right: you know the exact cartridge your faucet uses.

  2. Shut off the water and protect the sink

    Close both shut-off valves under the sink, open the faucet to drain it, and put a rag in the drain. Lay a towel in the sink to cushion dropped parts.

    Done right: the faucet is open and no water flows.

  3. Remove the handle and cap

    Pop off the decorative cap with a small flat screwdriver to reveal the handle screw, or find the hex set screw under the handle. Remove the screw and lift off the handle. Unscrew the dome cap or bonnet nut to expose the cartridge. Photograph every step.

    Done right: you can see the top of the cartridge and any retaining clip or nut.

  4. Pull out the old cartridge

    Note which way the cartridge's stem or tabs face; the new one must go in the same way or hot and cold will be reversed. Remove the retaining clip with needle-nose pliers or unscrew the retaining nut, then pull the cartridge straight up. Some Moen cartridges need a cartridge puller.

    Done right: the old cartridge is out and you have a photo of its orientation.

  5. Install the new cartridge

    Coat the new cartridge's O-rings with silicone faucet grease. Push it in with the same orientation as the old one, and reinstall the clip or nut. Put back the cap, handle and screw.

    Done right: the cartridge is seated fully and the handle moves smoothly through its full range.

  6. Turn the water on and test

    Open the shut-off valves slowly. Run the faucet hot and cold, then turn it off and watch the spout for a few minutes. If hot and cold are reversed, the cartridge stem needs to be turned 180 degrees.

    Done right: hot is on the left, cold on the right, and the spout doesn't drip.

Call a plumber if: the faucet leaks from its base or under the sink, the handle parts are corroded solid, or the faucet is old enough that parts aren't available. Replacing the whole faucet may then be the better option.

FAQ

Why does my single-handle faucet drip?

Most often the cartridge's seals are worn or mineral deposits have built up inside it. Replacing the cartridge usually stops the drip.

How do I know which cartridge to buy?

Identify the faucet brand and model, then match the cartridge part number. Bringing the old cartridge to the store also works.

Why are my hot and cold reversed after replacing the cartridge?

The cartridge went in rotated. Turn the water off, remove it, rotate it 180 degrees and reinstall.

Are faucet cartridges covered by warranty?

Many major brands offer lifetime warranties on cartridges for the original owner. Check with the manufacturer before buying a replacement.
